title: Mercury and the Sculptor
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: Mercury was very anxious to know in what estimation he was held by mankind; so he disguised himself as a man and walked into a Sculptor's studio, where there were a number of statues finished and ready for sale.

Seeing a statue of Jupiter among the rest, he inquired the price of it. "A crown," said the Sculptor. "Is that all?" said he, laughing; "and" (pointing to one of Juno) "how much is that one?" "That," was the reply, "is half a crown."

"And how much might you be wanting for that one over there, now?" he continued, pointing to a statue of himself. "That one?" said the Sculptor; "Oh, I'll throw him in for nothing if you'll buy the other two."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does Mercury disguise himself as a man?
options: He wants to buy a statue without being recognized as a god
He wants to test the Sculptor's honesty
He is anxious to know in what estimation he was held by mankind
He is hiding from another god

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where does Mercury walk into?
options: A Sculptor's studio
A crowded marketplace
A temple dedicated to Jupiter
A blacksmith's forge

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the price of the statue of Jupiter?
options: Half a crown
Two crowns
Nothing at all
A crown

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is the price of the statue of Juno?
options: A full crown
Half a crown
Two crowns
Three times the price of Jupiter's statue

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Mercury do when he hears the price of Jupiter's statue?
options: He immediately buys it
He argues that the price is too high
He laughs and asks about another statue
He walks away without saying anything

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sculptor say about the statue of Mercury himself?
options: That he'll throw it in for nothing if the buyer takes the other two
That it is the most expensive of the three
That it is not yet finished
That it is reserved for someone else

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Mercury ask about his own statue last?
options: He genuinely does not recognize the statue as himself
He wants to negotiate a discount on all three statues
He plans to buy only his own statue
He is building up to find out how mankind values him specifically

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Sculptor's answer reveal about how mankind values Mercury compared to Jupiter and Juno?
options: Mercury is seen as more valuable than either Jupiter or Juno
Mercury is seen as having little to no value on his own
Mercury is valued equally with Jupiter
Mercury's statue is too rare to be sold at all

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "estimation" mean in "in what estimation he was held by mankind"?
options: The exact price of an object
A formal written judgment
The regard or opinion others have of someone
A method of measuring height

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Vanity can lead someone to discover that they are valued less than they had hoped
Sculptors always undercharge for their best work
Mercury was the most respected of all the gods
Statues of gods should never be sold for money

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does Mercury find in the Sculptor's studio?
options: A single unfinished statue of himself
Tools used for carving stone
A crowd of customers already bargaining
A number of statues finished and ready for sale

questions.prompt: According to the passage, whose statue does Mercury ask about first?
options: Juno's
Jupiter's
His own
The Sculptor's

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does Mercury react upon hearing Jupiter's statue costs only a crown?
options: He immediately demands a lower price
He refuses to believe the Sculptor
He is surprised and asks, "Is that all?"
He asks to see a more expensive statue

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might Mercury have expected a higher price for Jupiter's statue?
options: Jupiter was considered the king of the gods, so a higher value might seem natural
He had seen similar statues sell for much more elsewhere
The Sculptor had a reputation for overpricing his work
He was told in advance what the statue should cost

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Sculptor's casual offer to "throw in" Mercury's statue sting more than a simple low price would?
options: It shows the Sculptor dislikes Mercury personally
It implies the statue is broken or damaged
It reveals that the Sculptor forgot to price it earlier
It suggests Mercury's statue has no value of its own at all, unlike the other two

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Sculptor would "throw in" the statue of Mercury?
options: Discard it as worthless and unsellable
Include it for free with another purchase
Sell it separately at a discount
Hide it from other customers

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: Mercury buys all three statues at a fair price
The Sculptor refuses to sell any of the statues to Mercury
Mercury disguises himself to learn his worth to mankind, and finds his own statue is valued at nothing
Mercury reveals his true identity to the Sculptor at the end
